title: Tall clock
medium: Cherry, mahogany with maple, white pine, yellow poplar

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1943

altText: A very tall wooden clock case that stands on the floor, with a clock face near the top, a long narrow middle section, and a wider base.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, maker, date, medium, region, dimensions, credit line, public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record

context: A floor-standing tall clock attributed in the Met record to James Dinsmore and dated 1803–9, made in New England. The Met lists cherry and mahogany with maple, white pine, and yellow poplar. It stands about 91 inches (232 cm) tall. Clocks like this were expensive household furnishings of the early United States.

descriptions.k: This clock is taller than most grown-ups. It stands on the floor. It has a clock face near the top and a long wooden body below. Do you know how a clock tells time?
descriptions.g12: This tall clock stands on the floor and is taller than a door. A clock face sits at the top, with a long wooden case below. It was made in New England more than two hundred years ago. Look for the face, the long middle, and the base. What parts do you see?
descriptions.g35: This tall clock was made in New England between 1803 and 1809. It stands on the floor and is more than seven feet tall. The wooden case has a top where the clock face sits, a long narrow middle, and a wider base. The Met lists several kinds of wood, including cherry and mahogany. Why do you think someone built a clock so large and so carefully?
descriptions.g68: In the early 1800s, a tall clock was both a useful machine and a prized piece of furniture. This one, made in New England between 1803 and 1809 and credited to James Dinsmore, stands about 91 inches tall. The wooden case frames the clock face and hides the moving parts. Mixed woods, including cherry and mahogany, show choices of material and cost. How does a clock's case turn timekeeping into a display of status and craftsmanship?
descriptions.g910: This tall clock from New England, dated 1803–9, shows how a timekeeping mechanism was housed in architecture-like furniture. The case is divided into hood, trunk, and base, and the Met lists a mix of woods, including cherry and mahogany, with maple, white pine, and yellow poplar. The vertical emphasis draws the eye up to the face, the focal point. Consider how cabinetmaker and clockmaker roles combined to make an object valued for both use and display.
descriptions.g1112: A tall clock such as this New England example of 1803–9 is a collaborative object in which the visible case and the hidden movement represent different trades and skills. The vertical, architectural form signals status in an era when accurate time was becoming a feature of private life. The wood mix recorded by the Met reflects cost, availability, and structure, with showy woods placed where they would be seen. Ask how such furniture reflects shifting ideas of time, wealth, and work in the early republic.

teacherNote.context: Tall case clocks combined a clockmaker's mechanism with a cabinetmaker's case and were status objects in early American homes. The Met record dates this one to 1803–9 and credits James Dinsmore.
directions: Have students measure their height against 91 inches and discuss how the clock's scale would feel in a room.
Ask students to draw the three sections of the case and label how each helps the clock work or look good.
Compare how time was kept in 1805 and today, and discuss what has changed in daily life.
